title: Esports In India Explained | BGMI, Free Fire, Asian Games And The New Law | Gaming Explained
description: Esports in India explained: the rise of mobile gaming, BGMI and Free Fire timelines, the Asian Games, 2026 tournaments and the 2025 online gaming law.

sections.heading: India the huge gaming nation
sections.script: India is one of the biggest gaming markets on Earth, and its esports scene is growing fast. In this video we explain esports in India, from the early days of cyber cafes to BGMI, Free Fire, the Asian Games and the new national law. We use Wikipedia's article on video gaming in India, reports from TechCrunch, Business Today and Outlook, and other news coverage, and we keep to dates and facts that sources agree on. According to the State of India Gaming report from Lumikai and Google, India had five hundred sixty eight million gamers as of November twenty twenty three. Most of them play on phones, which is why mobile titles dominate the scene. Let us look at how this all began.

sections.heading: From arcades to smartphones
sections.script: Gaming in India started in video game parlours with coin operated machines. In the nineteen nineties, eight bit Nintendo clones with cartridges arrived in homes, and later personal computers took over. In two thousand six, India had over one hundred thousand cyber cafes, and about forty percent of them were used for online games. Then smartphones changed everything. Wikipedia notes that India had seventy six million smartphone users in twenty thirteen and about six hundred ninety six million in twenty twenty. With cheap phones and cheap data, millions of people suddenly had a gaming device in their pocket. That is why esports in India grew mostly on mobile, not on consoles, and why battle royale games became so popular. Wikipedia also reports that India went from fifteen game studios in two thousand nine to two hundred seventy five by twenty twenty one, so the industry is growing on the development side too.

sections.heading: PUBG Mobile and the rise of BGMI
sections.script: The biggest name in Indian mobile esports was PUBG Mobile. In September twenty twenty, the Indian government banned PUBG Mobile along with one hundred seventeen other apps. Krafton then built a separate version for India, called Battlegrounds Mobile India, or BGMI. It was released on July second, twenty twenty one for Android and on August eighteenth, twenty twenty one for iOS. Fans adopted it quickly and BGMI tournaments became the centrepiece of the scene. BGMI quickly became the centre of the Indian mobile esports scene, and tournament organisers planned bigger events than ever before. For a short time, it looked unstoppable. Then the road got bumpy, as we will see next.

sections.heading: The break and the return
sections.script: In July twenty twenty two, Google removed BGMI from the Play Store in India after a government order, and Apple followed. That created a huge gap in the esports scene. Other mobile battle royale games, including Apex Legends Mobile and New State Mobile, could not fill it. In May twenty twenty three, Krafton announced that BGMI would return. TechCrunch reported that the government had granted a trial approval for three months after Krafton addressed concerns about data security and server location, and Business Today reported the return after a ban of about ten months. Different sources count the gap slightly differently, but all agree that BGMI came back, and tournaments restarted soon after.

sections.heading: Free Fire in India
sections.script: BGMI is not the only mobile title with a huge Indian following. Garena Free Fire was included among fifty four apps blocked by the Indian government in February twenty twenty two, and it left the Apple App Store and Google Play around February twelfth and thirteenth. Garena relaunched Free Fire in India in September twenty twenty three, with servers operated by Yotta, according to MediaNama, and cricketer MS Dhoni was named brand ambassador. Together, BGMI and Free Fire created the base of the mobile esports fan community in India, with separate leagues, teams and creators supporting each one.

sections.heading: The Asian Games and Indian esports
sections.script: Esports reached the biggest stage in Asia. At the twenty eighteen Jakarta Palembang Asian Games esports was a demonstration event, and India's Tirth Mehta won a bronze medal in Hearthstone. The Hangzhou Asian Games, held in September and October twenty twenty three after a postponement, made esports a medal sport. Seven titles were contested, including the mobile battle royale PUBG Mobile in a special Games version, plus Arena of Valor, Dota Two, League of Legends, EA Sports FC and Street Fighter Five, and India took part in four of them, Dota Two, EA Sports FC Online, League of Legends and Street Fighter Five Champion Edition. Esports has also been confirmed as a medal sport for the Aichi Nagoya Asian Games in twenty twenty six, so Indian players keep a path to a national flag.

sections.heading: Big tournaments in twenty twenty six
sections.script: Indian fans now enjoy a full tournament calendar. Krafton India runs the Battlegrounds Mobile India Series, called BGIS. Outlook Respawn reported that the BGIS twenty twenty six Grand Finals took place in Chennai, that iQOO Soul won the title, and that the final day reached more than six hundred thousand peak viewers. NODWIN Gaming runs the BGMI Masters Series, and Season Five was scheduled for August tenth to September sixth, twenty twenty six, at the NODWIN Gaming Arena in Delhi NCR, with sixteen teams in the Grand Finals and a prize pool of about one crore rupees. Prize money numbers vary between reports. For BGIS, figures from two crore to four crore rupees appear, depending on whether prize money unlocked by players through an in game initiative is counted, so check official pages for exact totals. The important point is that offline finals and large crowds are now normal.

sections.heading: A law that recognises esports
sections.script: There is also a new legal framework. The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, twenty twenty five, passed Parliament on August twenty first, twenty twenty five, and received Presidential assent on August twenty second. The law bans online money games, but it also empowers the Central Government to recognise and register esports as a legitimate sport. Under the definition, esports must be recognised under the National Sports Governance Act and registered with the designated authority. Prize money is allowed, but betting, wagering and staking are prohibited. Draft rules released in October twenty twenty five indicated that esports would fall under the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports. We could not confirm the final rules, so check official updates for the latest.

sections.heading: How to follow the scene safely
sections.script: If you want to enjoy Indian esports, start by watching the streams of the major tournaments on official YouTube channels. Learn the format. A battle royale tournament is scored with placement points and kill points across many matches, and the team with the highest total wins. Follow the teams, and read their announcements. If you want to play, remember that tournaments are competitive and demand hours of practice, so balance your game time with studies, sleep and exercise. And please avoid any betting or money based websites, since the law specifically prohibits wagering. Esports can lead to careers as players, coaches, analysts, casters and creators, but it begins with having fun and playing responsibly.

sections.heading: Where do you think Indian esports goes next
sections.script: Indian esports has come a long way. It started with cyber cafes and eight bit clones, grew through smartphones, survived app removals, reached the Asian Games, and now has a national law that names esports as a sport. The next step could be more offline arenas, more medals, and maybe an Indian team lifting a world title. What do you think? Will BGMI stay the king of Indian esports, or will another game take over?
